title: Two-dimensional motion: two 1D problems in parallel
explanation:
Throw a ball and its sideways and up-down motions do not interfere: motions along perpendicular axes are independent and can be analysed separately [1]. So a projectile is two 1D problems sharing one clock.

Horizontally, with negligible air resistance, there is no acceleration [2]: $x=v_x\,t$. Vertically, gravity gives a constant downward acceleration $g$: $v_y(t)=v_{y0}-g\,t$ and $y=v_{y0}\,t-\tfrac12 g\,t^2$.

The vertical motion sets the timing (when it peaks, when it lands), and the horizontal motion uses that time to find the distance. For a launch and landing at the same height, $y=0$ again at $t=\frac{2v_{y0}}{g}$.
keyIdeas: Split the motion into horizontal and vertical parts that share time $t$.
No drag: horizontal velocity is constant, $x=v_x t$.
Use the vertical motion to find the time, then the horizontal motion to find the range.

workedExample.problem: A ball is launched with $v_x=6$ m/s and $v_{y0}=25$ m/s and lands at launch height. With $g=10$ m/s² and no drag, find the flight time and range.
steps: Vertical: $y=25t-5t^2=t(25-5t)$, which is zero again at $t=5$ s.
Horizontal: the velocity stays 6 m/s for the whole flight.
Sanity check: the horizontal speed did not affect the flight time.

pitfalls: Letting the horizontal velocity change during the flight (no drag means no horizontal acceleration).
Using the total launch speed in the vertical equation instead of its vertical component.
Mixing signs: if up is positive, gravity's acceleration is negative.

citations.quote: The most important fact to remember here is that motions along perpendicular axes are independent and thus can be analyzed separately.
there is no acceleration along the horizontal axis when air resistance is negligible
